enrichment.short_title: Legal aid costs protection before certificate extension
key_facts: Mrs Frost had been legally aided since 1996 in Chancery proceedings against James Finlay Bank; the Bank's appeal to the Court of Appeal succeeded in May 2002 with a costs order against the claimant and potential liability for the Legal Services Commission.
The LSC disputed liability for Bank costs incurred before 26 November 2001, when the legal aid certificate was extended to cover the Court of Appeal appeal.
The Bank had prepared and served its notice of appeal and skeleton argument before the certificate extension, while the claimant remained funded throughout the underlying action.
The Costs Judge had to decide a preliminary point of dispute on whether costs protection applied to pre-extension appeal preparation costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment before a Costs Judge on a preliminary point of dispute as to the period for which the Legal Services Commission was liable for the successful unassisted appellant's Court of Appeal costs.
enrichment.outcome: Decision for the Bank; the LSC was liable to include Court of Appeal costs incurred before the certificate extension on 26 November 2001.
enrichment.ratio: Where a legally aided claimant remains in receipt of funded services throughout proceedings, costs protection under the Community Legal Service (Costs Protection) Regulations 2000 applies to Court of Appeal costs incurred before a formal certificate extension to cover the appeal, because the appeal formed part of funded proceedings and limiting recovery to post-extension costs would create unacceptable anomalies for opposing permission to appeal and preparing notices of appeal.
legal_issues: Whether Court of Appeal proceedings were funded proceedings before the certificate extension
The scope of costs protection under regulation 3(3) of the CP Regulations 2000
Whether regulation 5(4) limited recovery to costs attributable only to the appeal phase after extension
Application of S v S and Megarry v D J Ryan (No 2) to continuously funded litigation

enrichment.short_title: Late disability claim and IT1 pleading sufficiency
key_facts: Mr Argenio, a security steward of Italian origin employed by NEC Group, was dismissed in September 1999 after refusing at a meeting to confirm whether he was tape-recording proceedings.
His November 1999 IT1 claimed unfair dismissal and race discrimination; paragraph 5 mentioned dyslexia only as a reason for wanting to tape the meeting or have a note-taker.
In January 2001, shortly before trial, he sought to rely on disability discrimination based on dyslexia, more than a year out of time.
The employment tribunal and EAT refused to extend time; Sedley LJ granted limited permission to appeal on whether paragraph 5 sufficiently pleaded a DDA claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal with permission limited to whether facts in paragraph 5 of the originating application were capable of supporting a disability discrimination claim so as to avoid being out of time.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs summarily assessed at £10,000 inclusive of VAT.
enrichment.ratio: A broad, untechnical reading of an IT1 does not convert a passing reference to dyslexia—used only to explain why the claimant wanted to tape a meeting—into notification of a disability discrimination claim under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995; the January 2001 letter sought to introduce a new, time-barred complaint rather than relabel an existing claim.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 5 of the IT1 sufficiently notified a DDA 1995 claim
Just and equitable extension of time under section 8 and Schedule 3
Distinction between explaining conduct and pleading less favourable treatment by reason of disability
Application of Davidson v Ministry of Defence

enrichment.short_title: Future care damages: private home vs residential placement

statutes_considered.title: National Assistance Act 1948 (Choice of Accommodation) Directions 1992

key_facts: Louise Sowden suffered catastrophic brain injury aged 13 in a 1992 road accident and pursued damages through the Official Solicitor on 50% liability.
Parties agreed general damages, past losses, and future loss figures on both private and residential bases; the trial resolved which accommodation model should govern future damages.

The claimant had lived in residential settings for about ten years, valued privacy but had not clearly rejected shared residential care, and Dr Neumann supported shared accommodation with disabled young people.
Local authority residential care and awards under the National Assistance Act were disregarded in assessing liability to pay charges following Firth, Bell, and Ryan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial to assess damages for future losses after approved settlement on liability at 50% of full damages.
enrichment.outcome: Future damages assessed on a local authority residential arrangement basis, not on privately funded adapted accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: In assessing future care damages for a severely brain-injured claimant, the court must decide what arrangement is in the claimant's best interests rather than mirror pre-accident housing; where residential care with additional dedicated carer support meets her needs and a private arrangement would be experimental, disruptive, and not clearly superior, damages should not include the cost of private accommodation the local authority would otherwise provide under section 21 of the National Assistance Act 1948.
legal_issues: Private adapted home versus shared residential placement as the damages baseline
Whether local authority would fund equivalent private accommodation
Impact of 50% contributory negligence on affordability of private care
Disregard of damages and Court of Protection income for means-tested residential charges
Weight to be given to the claimant's expressed wishes

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 possession and historic sole tenancy discrimination
key_facts: Mrs O'Sullivan lived at 28 Bracewell Road as licensee of her husband, the sole secure tenant since a 1970 GLC grant reflecting common practice of naming husbands alone.
In March 2001 the husband validly determined the tenancy while the council reasonably believed the wife was not residing there; the tenancy was transferred to a smaller flat for the husband alone.
The property was the wife's article 8 home; the council sought possession after she refused a one-bedroom offer and sought to remain until rehousing under the homelessness queue.
The appeal was limited to articles 8 and 14 ECHR; the judge had granted possession subject to a stay pending appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a county court possession order, permitted on Convention grounds only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; possession order upheld, not to be executed before 15 April 2003; no order as to costs of appeal save assessment of second defendant's costs under the Access to Justice Act 1999.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority acts lawfully under the statutory housing scheme to recover possession from a trespassing spouse who was never a joint tenant, article 8(2) is satisfied at the macro level per Sheffield City Council v Smart and Wandsworth LBC v Michalak; article 14 is not violated because the appropriate comparator is a joint tenant whose co-tenant has terminated and transferred the tenancy, and the authority had no positive obligation to treat the appellant as a remaining joint tenant under its allocation policy before it knew she occupied the property.
legal_issues: Article 14 discrimination arising from historic sole tenancy to male spouses
Positive obligations under articles 8 and 14 to grant or treat as joint tenancy
Micro-level proportionality review in possession proceedings
Application of the joint tenancy termination policy in the Housing Allocation Scheme
Whether the court could defer eviction pending rehousing

enrichment.short_title: Professional negligence costs apportionment after trial
key_facts: Mr Moy's professional negligence claim against solicitors Pettman Smith and counsel Ms Pettman Smith had clear liability but was not settled until immediately before trial in April 2002, over three years after proceedings began.
The solicitors had from the outset sought to blame counsel via Part 20 proceedings; both indemnifiers resisted sensible ADR and settlement procedures.
At trial the court held counsel bore about 20% of the agreed damages; the parties disputed costs of the action, Part 20 proceedings, and the appeal.
On appeal, the solicitors abandoned root-and-branch challenges to liability findings but continued to dispute costs apportionment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judgment determining costs orders following trial and appeal in a solicitors' and counsel professional negligence action.
enrichment.outcome: Costs ordered as adjusted by Latham LJ: claimant's trial costs remain payable by solicitors; counsel pays 20% of solicitors' Part 20 and action costs below and two-thirds of solicitors' appeal costs; permission to appeal for counsel refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where solicitors unreasonably refused to settle a meritorious professional negligence claim promptly and instead pursued Part 20 blame against counsel, the court should not disturb an order that they pay the claimant's costs; as between co-defendants, costs should broadly follow the 20% liability split at trial, but on appeal a greater share of preparatory costs falls on counsel because much work related to abandoned grounds of appeal.
legal_issues: Apportionment of claimant's costs between solicitor and counsel defendants
Part 20 costs where settlement was unreasonably delayed
Effect of abandoning grounds of appeal on inter-partes costs
Whether Part 36 offer protected counsel on costs

enrichment.short_title: Section 139 bladed article reverse burden and Article 6
key_facts: Matthews was convicted by a 10:2 majority of having a bladed article in a public place contrary to section 139 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and sentenced to 60 hours' community service.
Police found a knife in his jacket pocket; he said at trial he carried it to cut lino for a friend but had not done so before arrest.
The judge directed the jury that Matthews bore a persuasive burden to prove good reason on the balance of probabilities.
The appeal challenged section 139 as an incompatible reverse burden under Article 6(2) ECHR, following R v Lambert and Lynch v DPP.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Crown Court appeal adjourned pending House of Lords petition in Lynch; judgment given after petition refused and further argument on Sheldrake v DPP.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 139(4) and (5) held compatible with Article 6(2) without read-down under section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998.
enrichment.ratio: Section 139(4) and (5) of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 impose a proportionate persuasive burden on the accused to prove good reason or lawful authority because the prosecution must prove knowing possession while the reason for carrying the blade is peculiarly within the accused's knowledge; unlike section 28 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, the lesser maximum sentence and different moral context justify maintaining the legal burden without incompatibility with the presumption of innocence.
legal_issues: Whether section 139 imposes a persuasive or evidential burden
Compatibility of reverse burden with Article 6(2) ECHR
Whether section 3 read-down is required
Distinction from R v Lambert and Sheldrake v DPP

confidence.notes: Full appellate judgment on Convention compatibility with clear dismissal and detailed Lambert analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Council market franchise and car boot sale injunction
key_facts: Leeds City Council sought final injunctions to stop Mr Watkins operating Sunday car boot sales at Drighlington and Morley without licence, within the common law 6⅔ mile market franchise distance from licensed Granary Wharf.
The Council held historic charter and statutory market rights preserved under the 1905 and 1980 Acts; interlocutory injunctions had stood since 1998.
Mr Watkins had previously been convicted under section 37 of the 1982 Act for an unlicensed Morley sale and knowingly continued operations; traffic concerns blocked licence applications.
He defended on Competition Act 1998 and EC Treaty articles 81 and 82 grounds and alleged NABMA collusion; expert market evidence was heavily criticised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of consolidated actions for permanent injunctions restraining unlicensed Sunday markets, with competition law counterclaims.
enrichment.outcome: Council's market rights established; final injunctions granted; defendant's counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority's franchise and statutory market rights are proprietary rights enforceable by injunction against same-day rival car boot sales within 6⅔ miles of an existing or licensed market; operating a post-1999 licensing regime to regulate commercial car boot sales does not, on the evidence, constitute an abuse of dominance or anti-competitive agreement, and refusal to grant injunctive relief on speculative future judicial review grounds would be disproportionate after a full trial.
legal_issues: Existence and scope of Leeds market franchise rights
Whether enforcement can rely on a licensed market at Granary Wharf
Chapter I and II Competition Act and articles 81 and 82 defences
Whether section 116 of the 1905 Act is a freestanding regulatory scheme
Discretionary refusal of injunction for alleged future illegality

enrichment.short_title: Housing benefit overpayment recovery and passport benefits

statutes_considered.title: Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000
Housing Benefit and Council Tax Benefit (Decisions and Appeals) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Mr McVeigh's housing benefit of about £109 per week paid to his landlord ended when jobseeker's allowance ceased on 23 October 2000; the authority sought to recover £769.86 overpayment from the landlord.
The Social Security Commissioner held landlords could not appeal against the authority's choice to recover from them rather than the claimant.
The Commissioner also held the authority must not terminate housing benefit until it had assessed offset under regulation 104 for continuing entitlement.
The Secretary of State appealed; neither the local authority nor the landlord appeared in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal under Schedule 7 to the Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000 against a Commissioner's decision on housing benefit overpayment recovery.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on both issues; Commissioner's decision set aside and matter remitted to an appeal tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord from whom a local authority decides to recover a housing benefit overpayment under regulation 101 has a right of appeal to a tribunal against that discretionary choice, not merely against recoverability in principle; separately, entitlement to housing benefit ends when a passport benefit ceases under regulation 67(1)(a), and any reduction of the recoverable overpayment under regulation 104 is a distinct calculation that does not postpone termination of the benefit period.
legal_issues: Tribunal jurisdiction over discretion to recover overpayment from landlord versus claimant
Construction of regulation 101 and Schedule 7 paragraph 6(6)
Whether housing benefit must continue pending regulation 104 offset assessment
Effect of cessation of jobseeker's allowance on benefit period

enrichment.short_title: Quantum meruit after dishonest assistance in secret commissions
key_facts: A L Barnes Ltd fitted out mobile phone retail outlets for Time Talk (UK) Ltd on a quantum meruit basis under the Time Talk Project after no price was agreed.
A secret 1997 arrangement required Barnes to inflate invoices to include project manager Andrew Craft's fees, paid on to him after Barnes received payment from Time Talk director John Colbert.

The judge found Barnes director Robert Gibson dishonestly assisted Colbert and Craft in breach of fiduciary duty to Time Talk under Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan, but allowed recovery for work done excluding project management fees (£15,250) and upheld a counterclaim of £87,003.72.
Time Talk appealed arguing the entire quantum meruit claim was tainted by illegality; Barnes cross-appealed on costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal and cross-appeal following county court trial on quantum meruit claim and illegality/defence based on dishonest assistance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal on costs allowed in part—Time Talk to pay 25% of Barnes' costs on claim and counterclaim on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: Where shop-fitting contracts are quantum meruit claims for work actually done and accepted, a secret commission arrangement between an employee, project manager, and contractor is not an integral part of the contract so as to render the whole claim unenforceable for illegality; the contractor may recover reasonable remuneration for executed work but not sums representing doubly paid project management fees, and Dyson v Time Group binds the court to reject imputation of the employee's knowledge to defeat the claim.
legal_issues: Whether illegality or dishonest assistance bars the entire quantum meruit claim
Severability of secret commission element from main contract
Application of Taylor v Bhail and Mohammed v Alaga & Co
Comparative culpability and less culpable party recovery
Who is the successful party for costs where judgment net of counterclaim favours claimant

enrichment.short_title: Structure plan gypsy site policy and Panel recommendation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999
Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Mrs Butler, a Romany gypsy, challenged the adopted 2002 Avon replacement structure plan under section 287, focusing on Policy 37 on gypsy and traveller site provision.

Panel recommendation R21 after examination in public required separate structure plan policy requiring suitable locations to be identified in local plans, reflecting failure of criteria-only approaches.
The joint planning committee adopted Policy 37 allowing local plans to secure appropriate site provision by locational or criteria-based policies, without treating this as departing from R21.
The claimant alleged breach of regulation 15(4) for failing to invite objections where the authorities did not accept the Panel recommendation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 application to quash the joint structure plan within six weeks of adoption, with permission to amend the claim form granted at hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; permission to appeal refused; no order as to costs subject to public funding assessment.
enrichment.ratio: It was reasonably open to the joint structure plan authorities to interpret Panel recommendation R21 as permitting local plans either to identify specific gypsy sites or apply criteria-based policies depending on local circumstances, consistent with Circular 1/94; because they subjectively did not intend to depart from R21, regulation 15(4) of the 1999 Regulations did not require a further objection procedure, applying the Woods principle that planning policy construction is for the authority if reasonably available.
legal_issues: Whether R21 mandated site-specific allocation rather than criteria-based local plan policies
Breach of regulation 15(4) when authorities reserve judgment on a Panel recommendation
Whether the whole structure plan or only Policy 37 should be quashed if procedural breach found
Relationship of Policy 37 to Circular 1/94 and PPG12
